title-group.article-title: Temporal Interference Stimulation of Centromedian‐Parafascicular Complex in Disorders of Consciousness: A Pilot Study

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Treatment of disorders of consciousness (DoC) remains a major clinical challenge, and noninvasive, targeted modulation of deep brain structures has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. We aimed to evaluate the feasibility/safety and preliminary effects of thalamic temporal interference stimulation (TIS) targeting centromedian‐parafascicular (CM‐PF) complex in patients with DoC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted a single‐arm, self‐controlled trial in nine patients with DoC. All patients received TIS targeting the bilateral CM‐PF complex once daily for 10 consecutive days. Stimulation targets were guided by patient‐specific electric field modeling to ensure precise neuromodulation. Outcome measures included adverse events, the change in Coma Recovery Scale‐Revised (CRS‐R) total and subscale scores from baseline to after five and 10 stimulation sessions, and alterations in EEG “ABCD” patterns and power spectral density (PSD) following the tenth session.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: No serious adverse events were reported. After 10 stimulation sessions, CRS‐R total scores increased significantly, with improvements primarily observed in the auditory, visual, and motor subscales. No significant changes in CRS‐R scores were detected after five stimulation sessions. EEG analyses demonstrated an increased prevalence of patterns C and D, disappearance of pattern A, and elevated global PSD in the alpha and beta frequency bands after 10 stimulation sessions.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: This pilot study demonstrates that thalamic TIS is a safe and feasible noninvasive deep brain stimulation technology that may facilitate consciousness recovery in patients with DoC. Larger randomized controlled trials with longer follow‐up are needed to confirm these preliminary observations.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Disorders of consciousness (DoC) usually follow severe brain injury due to trauma, anoxia, or stroke, and are characterized by marked impairments in awareness and/or arousal [1]. When these conditions persist for more than 28 days, they are classified as prolonged DoC (pDoC), including vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS) and minimally conscious state (MCS) [2]. Patients with pDoC show profound limitations in communication and purposeful behavior, require long‐term institutional or home‐based care, and impose a considerable burden on families and healthcare systems [3, 4]. Despite the use of multiple therapeutic strategies to promote recovery of consciousness and functional improvement, only a small proportion of patients with DoC derive substantial benefit and achieve meaningful restoration of consciousness [5]. This therapeutic gap underscores the need for novel approaches that can reliably enhance arousal and awareness.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has emerged as a promising option for selected patients with pDoC [6]. By delivering electrical stimulation to deep nuclei such as the centromedian–parafascicular (CM‐PF) complex, central thalamus and globus pallidus internus, DBS can modulate thalamo‐striatal and thalamo‐cortical circuits that are central to conscious processing [7, 8, 9, 10]. The CM and PF receive rich inputs from the brainstem ascending reticular activating system, the internal segment of the globus pallidus, and the reticular part of the substantia nigra (the output nuclei of the basal ganglia), and then project strongly to sensorimotor cortical areas as well as the prefrontal and cingulate cortices [11]. Because these structures are critically involved in arousal and cognition, the CM‐PF complex plays a central role in neuromodulation for disorders of consciousness. Supporting this, sEEG evidence from the human brain supports that the intralaminar and medial thalamic nuclei, particularly the CM‐PF complex, act as gatekeepers for prefrontal cortical activity during conscious perception through thalamofrontal synchrony and cross‐frequency coupling [12]. Furthermore, in 40 patients with DoC who underwent DBS targeting the CM‐PF complex, electric field modeling reveals that stimulation is most effective when it extends below the CM nucleus to engage the inferior PF nucleus and the adjacent ventral tegmental tract, compared to other regions [13]. However, DBS requires stereotactic surgery, carries perioperative risks, and is associated with high costs and limited availability. These constraints substantially restrict its use in routine care and motivate the search for noninvasive alternatives that can target similar deep structures.

Temporal interference (TI) stimulation is a recently developed, noninvasive electrical neuromodulation technique designed to focally modulate deep brain regions in humans [14]. TI applies two high‐frequency alternating currents, usually above 1 kHz, with slightly different frequencies through scalp electrodes. These currents pass through the skull with relatively low attenuation [15]. In the region where the two fields overlap, they generate a low‐frequency amplitude‐modulated envelope that can effectively drive neural activity, while superficial and off‐target regions primarily experience high‐frequency components that are less effective at depolarizing neurons. This mechanism allows selective engagement of deep targets with limited stimulation of overlying cortex and reduced discomfort, addressing a major limitation of conventional noninvasive stimulation methods.

Accumulating evidence suggests that temporal interference stimulation (TIS) is safe in humans and can modulate deep networks in a functionally meaningful way [16, 17, 18, 19]. Hippocampal TIS has been reported to improve episodic memory and increase hippocampal activation [16], and theta‐burst patterned TIS over the striatum has been shown to enhance motor learning and strengthen motor network connectivity in older adults [17]. However, the potential of TIS to promote recovery in pDoC has not been systematically explored.

In this pilot study, we developed an individualized TIS protocol targeting the CM‐PF complex and evaluated its safety and efficacy in patients with pDoC. We aimed to determine whether noninvasive TIS of the thalamus can promote behavioral signs of consciousness and modulate relevant brain networks in this highly treatment‐resistant population.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This was a single‐group, pre–post interventional trial conducted at the Coma Awakening Center, Department of Neurology, Xijing Hospital, Xi'an, China. The overall study design is shown in Figure 1.

caption.p: Study flow diagram. CM‐PF, centromedian‐parafascicular; CRS‐R, Coma Recovery Scale‐Revised; MCS, minimally conscious state; TI, temporal interference; TIS, temporal interference stimulation; VS/UWS, vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome.

sec.title: Subjects/Recruitment
sec.p: Inclusion criteria were: (1) age 18 to 80 years; (2) diagnosis of vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS) or minimally conscious state (MCS) based on Coma Recovery Scale–Revised (CRS‐R) assessments during the screening period; (3) more than 28 days since brain injury; (4) acquired brain injury of known etiology; and (5) informed consent provided by a legal surrogate.

Exclusion criteria were: (1) continuous use of sedative medications, sodium or calcium channel blockers, or NMDA receptor antagonists; (2) history of severe or progressive neurological disease; (3) history of epilepsy or ongoing seizures; (4) unstable vital signs or other life‐threatening medical conditions; (5) skull defect or active implanted device (such as cardiac pacemaker or defibrillator, deep brain stimulator, ventriculoperitoneal shunt); and (6) documented pregnancy.

sec.title: Standard Protocol Approvals, Registrations, and Subject Consents
sec.p: The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines, was approved by the Ethics Committee of Xijing Hospital (KY20242231‐F‐1), and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06851156). Written informed consent was obtained from each patient's legal surrogate.

sec.title: Individualized Temporal Interference Modeling
sec.p: Subject‐specific temporal interference (TI) models were generated using NervioX‐S2400 software (2024). Two sinusoidal currents at 2.050 kHz and 2.000 kHz were applied, yielding an envelope frequency Δf of 50 Hz in the target region.

First, T1‐weighted structural MRI images were segmented with SPM12 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/) into six tissue classes with assigned conductivities: scalp (0.465 S/m), skull (0.010 S/m), cerebrospinal fluid (1.650 S/m), white matter (0.126 S/m), gray matter (0.276 S/m), and cavities (2.5 × 10−14 S/m). The international 10–10 EEG electrode system was then registered onto each participant's scalp. Tetrahedral finite element meshes were generated using the Computational Geometry Algorithms Library (CGAL). Using the finite element solver GetDP, we computed the electric field generated by each electrode pair separately. TI field strength was then derived according to the TI coupling principle. The AAL3 atlas was registered to each participant's MRI to identify the CM‐PF region of the thalamus (Figure S1) [20]. For each participant, an exhaustive search was used to determine the electrode montage that maximized the TI field intensity within the CM‐PF.

sec.title: CM‐PF‐TIS Stimulation Paradigm
sec.p: Stimulation was delivered using a transcranial electrical stimulator (TES NEURO‐800, Neurodome Inc., China) for 10 consecutive days. Based on the indication provided in DBS for DoC treatment [21], the bilateral CM‐PF was targeted. Each daily session consisted of 60 min of TI stimulation with a fixed left‐then‐right order (30 min targeting the left CM‐PF, followed by 30 min targeting the right CM‐PF). All patients received TIS while lying semi‐recumbent in a quiet, separate room without concurrent treatments [22]. Arousal was continuously monitored, and patients were kept awake using the arousal procedures from the CRS‐R throughout the stimulation periods whenever possible. These conditions were kept consistent across all sessions and patients.

sec.title: Clinical Assessment
sec.p: The CRS‐R is the standard clinical tool to assess the level of consciousness and to distinguish between coma, VS/UWS, MCS, and emergence from MCS (EMCS) [23, 24]. It comprises six subscales evaluating auditory, visual, motor, oromotor/verbal, communication, and arousal functions, with a maximum total score of 23. Higher scores indicate higher levels of consciousness.

During the one‐week screening period, each patient underwent five CRS‐R assessments on separate days, administered at the bedside by two independent and experienced clinicians at standardized time points (9:00–11:00 AM) [25]. Diagnoses of VS/UWS and MCS were based on specific CRS‐R subscale items [24]. During the intervention phase, the CRS‐R was administered before the first stimulation session and after the fifth and tenth sessions. All assessments were performed with patients' eyes open in a familiar setting in the absence of environmental interference, and an arousal‐promoting protocol was applied if eyes were closed.

sec.title: EEG Data Acquisition and Preprocessing
sec.p: EEG was recorded with 32 Ag/AgCl ring electrodes connected to a BrainAmp MR Plus amplifier (Brain Products GmbH, Gilching, Germany), with electrodes placed according to the international 10–20 system. Signals were sampled at 1000 Hz and impedances were kept below 5 kΩ. Continuous EEG was collected for 20–30 min immediately before the first stimulation session and immediately after the completion of the tenth stimulation session. Participants were maintained in an awake, eyes‐open state; if eye closure or drowsiness was observed, an arousal protocol was applied as recommended by the CRS‐R scale [23].

EEG preprocessing was implemented using the EEGLAB in custom Matlab R2023a. The EEG signal was filtered between 0.5 and 70 Hz and notch‐filtered at 50 Hz to remove line noise, and then downsampled to 500 Hz. Prior to preprocessing, the data were visually inspected to exclude drowsy or eyes‐closed periods, as well as segments with large‐amplitude movement artifacts. First, bad channels were removed and interpolated using spherical spline interpolation. Then, independent component analysis was applied to identify artifact components, which were subsequently removed manually. Finally, the data were visually inspected again to eliminate any residual segments not adequately cleaned in the previous steps. All signals were re‐referenced to the average of the mastoids before feature extraction. The entire preprocessing pipeline was standardized and semi‐automated, applied identically to each recording.

sec.title: Power Spectral Analysis
sec.p: EEG power was analyzed for canonical frequency bands using monopolar montages, both for the whole brain and across brain lobes: frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal, and central. The frequency bands included delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), low gamma (30–50 Hz), and high gamma (50–70 Hz). Power spectral density (PSD) was estimated using Welch's method with a Hamming window and 50% overlap. All spectral analyzes were performed in MATLAB (MathWorks) using EEGLAB toolboxes.

sec.title: ‘ABCD’ EEG Pattern Analysis
sec.p: To characterize neurophysiological changes associated with TI stimulation, we applied the “ABCD” EEG pattern framework based on EEG power. This model describes a potential sequence of EEG phenotypes reflecting the severity of thalamo‐cortical deafferentation and has been proposed as a marker of conscious processing in DoC. The patterns are defined as: (A) Frequencies below 4 Hz, indicating complete or near‐complete deafferentation of the neocortex resulting from structural injuries; (B) Narrow‐band theta activity (4–7 Hz) suggesting severe deafferentation generated by layer V pyramidal neurons under hyperpolarized neocortical membrane potentials; (C) Mixed theta and beta activity suggesting moderate deafferentation with partial recovery of neocortical membrane potentials and synchronous bursting of thalamic neurons; (D) Near‐normal cortical activity characterized by prominent alpha and beta rhythms. Each EEG recording was assigned an ABCD category to track changes in thalamo‐cortical dynamics across sessions.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: Safety outcomes include, but are not limited to, seizures or epileptiform activity, autonomic instability, agitation or behavioral intolerance, interruptions of stimulation, skin discomfort or burns, and worsening of EEG findings or other adverse neurophysiological changes. Efficacy outcomes include the effect of TIS on CRS‐R total score assessed at three time points (baseline, Day 5 and Day 10), as well as its effect on CRS‐R subscale scores (auditory, visual, motor, oromotor/verbal, communication, arousal). Additional outcomes comprise pre–post changes in log‐transformed EEG power within each frequency band and changes in the ordinal ABCD EEG pattern. Safety was evaluated by monitoring adverse events throughout the study.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All statistical tests were two‐sided, with a significance threshold of α = 0.05. The primary efficacy outcome was the effect of visit on the CRS‐R total score across three assessments (Baseline, Day 5, and Day 10). Secondary efficacy outcomes included time effects on CRS‐R subscales (auditory, visual, motor, oromotor/verbal, communication, and arousal), changes in EEG log‐power between Baseline and Day 10 within canonical frequency bands (delta, 1–4 Hz; theta, 4–8 Hz; alpha, 8–13 Hz; beta, 13–30 Hz; low gamma, 30–50 Hz; and high gamma, 50–70 Hz), and changes in the ordinal ABCD‐mode.

CRS‐R outcomes were analyzed using time‐only linear mixed‐effects models (LMMs) with subject‐specific random intercepts and time as a categorical fixed effect. Primary inference focused on the overall effect of time, followed by prespecified pairwise contrasts comparing Day 5 and Day 10 with Baseline, reported as estimated marginal mean differences. A covariate‐adjusted LMM including age, sex, etiology, and time since injury was fitted as a sensitivity analysis. Additional sensitivity analyses used the Friedman test for omnibus within‐subject visit effects and paired Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests (two‐sided; exact p values where feasible) for pairwise comparisons. The arousal subscale was not analyzed inferentially because all patients had the same score at all three visits.

EEG power values were log‐transformed before analysis. For each frequency‐region measure, Baseline‐to‐Day 10 EEG changes were analyzed using time‐only LMMs with subject‐specific random intercepts and visit as a fixed effect. Covariate‐adjusted LMMs including age, sex, etiology, and time since injury, as well as paired Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests, were performed as sensitivity analyses. Because multiple EEG frequency‐region measures were examined, these analyses were considered exploratory and interpreted cautiously.

Changes in the ordinal ABCD‐mode index between Baseline and Day 10 were assessed using the paired Wilcoxon signed‐rank test (two‐sided). This non‐parametric approach was chosen because the limited sample size and sparse distribution of ordinal scores precluded stable regression‐based modeling.
All analyses were conducted in R (v4.5.0), using lme4 for LMM fitting, lmerTest for inference, emmeans for estimated marginal means and pairwise contrasts, and ggplot2 for visualization.

sec.title: Baseline Demographic and Clinical Characteristics
sec.p: From 20 May 2025 to 10 October 2025, nine patients were enrolled. The median age was 54.0 years (IQR 38.5–61.5), and 8 of 9 (88.9%) were male. At enrollment, the median time since brain injury was 42.0 days (IQR 35.0–53.5). The median baseline CRS‐R total score was 5.0 (IQR 5.0–7.0). Eight patients (88.9%) were in a VS/UWS, and one patient was in a MCS. Etiologies included anoxia (n = 4), stroke (n = 4), and traumatic brain injury (n = 1). Medication (5 patients received oral baclofen) and rehabilitation were kept unchanged throughout the experiment. The clinical characteristics and lesion features are shown in Tables 1 and S1.

sec.title: The Effects of TIS on Consciousness
sec.p: The TIS montage and stimulation settings were computationally determined based on each individual's structural brain MRI data (Table S2). After 10 stimulation sessions, TIS was associated with a significant increase in CRS‐R total score (difference 2.44, 95% CI 1.20–3.69, p = 0.001), particularly in the auditory (difference 0.78, 95% CI 0.32–1.24, p = 0.004), visual (difference 0.67, 95% CI 0.21–1.12, p = 0.011), and motor subscales (difference 0.78, 95% CI 0.15–1.41, p = 0.028) (Table 2). No significant changes in CRS‐R total or subscale scores were detected after five sessions. Three patients showed behavioral signs of improved consciousness after 10 treatment sessions: two transitioned from VS/UWS to MCS−, and one progressed from MCS− to EMCS (Table S1). The arousal subscale was not analyzed inferentially because all patients had the same score at all three visits. Individual CRS‐R trajectories are shown in Figures S2 and S3.

caption.p: Estimated changes in CRS‐R total and subscale scores over time based on linear mixed‐effects models.

fn.p: Note: Estimates and p values were obtained from linear mixed‐effects models with time as the only fixed effect and subject‐specific random intercepts. Median values with interquartile range (IQR) are shown. The bold values in the table indicate statistical significance.
All patients scored 2 on the Arousal subscale at all three time points; the LMM could not estimate variance components for this outcome.

sec.p: Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of these findings. In the covariate‐adjusted linear mixed‐effects models, the time‐effect estimates were essentially unchanged, and the improvements at Day 10 remained significant for the CRS‐R total, auditory, visual, and motor scores (Table S3). In the non‐parametric sensitivity analyses, Friedman tests showed significant overall differences across the three visits for the CRS‐R total score (χ 2 = 12, p = 0.002) as well as the auditory (χ 2 = 8.000, p = 0.018), visual (χ 2 = 7, p = 0.030), and motor subscales (χ 2 = 7.538, p = 0.023) (Table S4).

Pairwise Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests further confirmed significant increases in CRS‐R total score from Baseline to Day 10 (p = 0.016) and from Day 5 to Day 10 (p = 0.016), whereas pairwise comparisons for individual subscales did not reach significance, consistent with the more conservative nature of the non‐parametric analyses (Table S5).
TIS targeting the CM‐PF complex was generally well tolerated. No serious adverse events occurred, and only one patient developed mild local swelling at the electrode sites.

sec.title: The Effects of TIS on EEG
sec.p: Eight patients completed EEG examination. After the tenth session, TIS was associated with a significant shift in the distribution of ABCD EEG patterns (p = 0.012; Figure 2A), with an increased prevalence of patterns C and D and disappearance of pattern A. In the primary linear mixed‐effects analyses, stimulation was associated with increased global EEG log‐power in the alpha (estimate 0.534, p = 0.027) and beta (estimate 0.700, p = 0.035) bands, whereas changes in delta, theta, low‐gamma, and high‐gamma bands were not statistically significant, although theta and low‐gamma showed trend‐level increases (p = 0.072 for both) (Table S6). Region‐specific analyses showed significant increases in theta power over the occipital (p = 0.044) and central (p = 0.028) regions; alpha power over the frontal (p = 0.031), parietal (p = 0.024), occipital (p = 0.026), temporal (p = 0.016), and central (p = 0.042) regions; beta power over the frontal (p = 0.025), parietal (p = 0.027), and temporal (p = 0.018) regions; and low‐gamma power over the parietal region (p = 0.043) (Table S6; Figure 2B–I). Individual EEG trajectories are shown in Figures S4 and S5.

caption.p: EEG changes after 10 sessions of CM–PF temporal interference stimulation. (A) Differences in the distribution of “ABCD” EEG patterns after 10 stimulation sessions. (B–G) Differences in global power spectral density after 10 stimulation sessions in the delta (B), theta (C), alpha (D), beta (E), low gamma (F), and high gamma (G) frequency bands. (H, I) Differences in alpha (H) and beta (I) power across the frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal, and central lobes.

sec.p: These EEG findings were partly supported by sensitivity analyses. In the covariate‐adjusted models, the global alpha (p = 0.040) and beta (p = 0.049) increases remained significant, together with regional increases in theta power over the central region (p = 0.038); alpha power over the frontal (p = 0.045), parietal (p = 0.035), occipital (p = 0.038), and temporal (p = 0.025) regions; and beta power over the frontal (p = 0.037), parietal (p = 0.039), and temporal (p = 0.028) regions (Table S7). In the paired Wilcoxon signed‐rank analyses, significant increases were observed for alpha power over the occipital (p = 0.042) and temporal (p = 0.021) regions and for beta power over the frontal (p = 0.042) and temporal (p = 0.042) regions, whereas the global alpha and beta effects were reduced to trend level (p = 0.059 for both) (Table S8). Taken together, these analyses suggest that the EEG effects were directionally consistent across methods, although the number of significant findings was smaller in the more conservative sensitivity analyzes.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This pilot, single‐arm trial suggests that 10 sessions of individualized 50 Hz TIS designed to target the bilateral CM‐PF are feasible and can be well tolerated in patients with pDoC. The preliminary evidence suggests that this noninvasive deep brain stimulation may facilitate short‐term improvement in consciousness recovery and enhance thalamo‐cortical integrity.

The improvement in consciousness observed with noninvasive TIS was comparable in direction to that reported with invasive DBS. Thalamic DBS, particularly targeting the CM‐PF complex, has previously shown therapeutic potential in patients with pDoC [11, 26]. A systematic review of 21 studies involving 146 patients with DoC revealed that CM‐PF was the most commonly targeted nucleus of DBS, with 50 Hz identified as the most effective stimulation frequency [9]. Furthermore, a DBS study targeting the bilateral CM‐PF reported that 47.8% (11/23) of patients exhibited improved levels of consciousness after 12 months of follow‐up, including 38.5% (5/13) of those initially diagnosed with VS/UWS who progressed to MCS or EMCS [21]. Of note, specific electrophysiological features of the CM‐PF were found to be associated with more favorable clinical outcomes. In our cohort, 88.9% of patients were initially classified as VS/UWS, and 25% progressed to MCS− after 10 days of TIS. Although the direction of improvement is consistent, the observed efficacy differs between the two approaches, likely due to differences in stimulation duration, follow‐up length, and baseline consciousness levels.

Several mechanisms may account for the role of CM‐PF stimulation in promoting conscious awareness. Anatomically, the CM‐PF complex maintains extensive connections with cortical and subcortical regions implicated in consciousness, including the striatum and neocortex [27, 28, 29]. Functionally, thalamo‐cortical circuits involving the CM‐PF and mediodorsal magnocellular nuclei are considered essential for conscious perception [12]. In addition, bilateral CM‐PF stimulation, as implemented in this study, may induce stronger and more widespread cortical activation than unilateral stimulation paradigms applied in other neurological conditions [30].

In patients with severe traumatic brain injury, EEG spectral and ABCD classifications improve longitudinally in parallel with behavioral recovery and correlate with the behavioral level of consciousness in both the acute and subacute‐to‐chronic phases [31]. Our EEG findings are descriptively compatible with the hypothesis that TIS targeting CM‐PF complex may improve network organization (e.g., increased prevalence of “C”/“D” patterns and higher alpha/beta power) [32, 33]. Improvement in the ABCD EEG pattern may reflect restoration of thalamo‐cortical integrity. However, given the absence of a control group and the well‐known susceptibility of EEG signals to fluctuations in arousal and vigilance, these results should be interpreted as exploratory and supportive rather than as confirmation of a specific mechanism.

As a pilot study, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the single‐arm design, small sample size, and absence of a control group limit the ability to exclude confounding factors and preclude causal inference, and the mix of different etiologies and consciousness levels limits the generalizability and interpretability of our findings. Moreover, improvements in consciousness may be attributable not only to spontaneous recovery but also to non‐specific stimulation and environmental effects. Therefore, future studies should employ large‐sample designs with a sham control. Second, the lack of evoked physiological assessments (such as SEP, MMN, P300, and TMS‐EEG) and functional MRI in the current study precludes more direct evidence of altered network responsiveness. Although individualized electric field modeling provides anatomical guidance for targeting, it does not directly confirm actual modulation of CM‐PF neurons, which remains an inherent limitation of the present study. Future animal experiments should combine TI stimulation with chemogenetic or optogenetic manipulation of the CM‐PF nucleus to establish whether the arousal‐promoting effects of TI in patients with DoC are specifically mediated by altered CM‐PF neural activity, rather than merely reflecting a non‐specific current network effect. Nevertheless, prior studies using electric field modeling and measurements in human cadavers have provided converging evidence that temporal interference stimulation can be focused on deep brain structures such as the hippocampus [16], supporting the plausibility of our targeting strategy. Third, the study was limited to short‐term therapeutic effects and did not include long‐term functional outcome measures. Consequently, we cannot draw any conclusions regarding the persistence of the observed effects. Future trials integrating both short‐term changes in consciousness and long‐term functional recovery will be essential to determine the durability and clinical relevance of TIS effects.

In summary, this pilot, single‐arm, self‐controlled trial indicates that individualized 50 Hz TIS targeting the thalamic CM‐PF region is feasible and may offer a promising approach to improving consciousness in patients with DoC. However, due to the pilot nature and limited sample size, these observations warrant cautious interpretation.
